## Column 4

"...to their husbands, from the poor to the rich." 

This advice pleased the king and the rulers, and the king did exactly as Muchaios had spoken. He sent letters into all the kingdom, to every province according to their own language, so that there would be respect for the men <note>original: φόβον (fear/reverence)</note> in their own homes. <margin>This marginal note corrects the text to clarify that the decree was sent to every land according to its speech.</margin> 

After these events, the king’s anger subsided. He no longer remembered Vashti, but he did remember what she had said and how he had condemned her. Then the king’s servants said, "Let beautiful young virgins be sought for the king. Let the king appoint commissioners <note>original: κωμάρχας (village leaders or local officials)</note> in all the provinces of his kingdom, and let them select beautiful young virgins for the city of Susa. 

Let them be brought to the harem <note>original: γυναικῶνα (women's quarters)</note> and handed over to the king’s eunuch who guards the women. Then, let beauty treatments <note>original: σμῆγμα (cleansing agents or ointments)</note> be given to them."

## Column 2

~ Esther and the Kingdom ~ <note>This header was added by a later scribe to indicate the start of the book's main narrative</note>

Mordecai rested in the courtyard with Gabatha and Tharra, the two eunuchs of the king who guarded the courtyard. He heard their discussions and investigated their schemes, learning that they were preparing to lay hands on King Artaxerxes. 

Mordecai reported them to the king. The king then interrogated the two eunuchs, and after they confessed, they were led away to be executed. The king wrote these events in his records as a memorial, and Mordecai also wrote about these matters. 

The king then ordered Mordecai to serve in the courtyard and gave him gifts for his service. However, Haman son of Hammedatha, a <term>Bougaean</term> <note>original: Βουγαῖος; a title of uncertain meaning, possibly "bully" or a corruption of "Agagite"</note>, who was highly honored in the king's presence, sought to harm Mordecai and his people because of what had happened to the king's two eunuchs.

And after this, having shown them the wealth of his kingdom and the glory of his abundance and joy for one hundred and eighty days, and when the days of the wedding feast <note>original: γάμου; though contextually a general celebration, the Greek uses the word for wedding</note> were completed, the king gave a banquet for the nations present in the city. ## Column 4

The courtyard was decorated with fine linen and cotton hangings stretched on cords of fine linen and purple. These were fastened to gold and silver cubes set upon pillars of Parian marble and stone. There were couches of gold and silver placed on a mosaic floor of emerald, pearl, and Parian stone. There were patterned coverings, and roses were scattered all around. 

The drinking vessels were made of gold and silver, and a small <term>carbuncle</term> <note>original: ἀνθρακος; a deep red gemstone, likely a ruby or garnet</note> cup made of precious gold was displayed. There was an abundance of sweet wine, the kind that the king himself drank. This banquet was not conducted according to any restrictive law; for the king desired it so, and he ordered the stewards to fulfill his own will and the will of the guests. 

Also, Queen <term>Vashti</term> <note>original: Αστὶν (Astin)</note> gave a banquet for the women in the palace where King Artaxerxes lived.

The scribes were called in the first month, which is Nisan <note>original: Νισὰν; the Hebrew text specifies Sivan, the third month, but this Greek manuscript records Nisan, the first month</note>, on the twenty-third day of the same year. Everything was written exactly as Mordecai <margin>Mordecai...</margin> commanded to the administrators and the rulers of the provinces, from India to Ethiopia—one hundred and twenty-seven provinces in total. The orders were sent to each province and each nation, and specifically to the Jews, in their own language. 

The decree was written in the name of the king and sealed with his signet ring. They sent out the letters by couriers <note>original: βιβλιαφόρων; literally "book-bearers" or letter-carriers</note>. ## Column 2

<margin>To all the rulers of the provinces and to those who are loyal to our interests: Greetings.</margin>
twenty-seven provinces from India to Ethiopia: Greetings.

Many people, who have been honored too often by the great kindness of their benefactors, have become arrogant. Not only do they seek to harm our subjects, but being unable to handle such abundance <note>original: κόρον; literally "satiety" or "excess," implying they are spoiled by power</note>, they even attempt to plot against their own benefactors. They not only remove gratitude from among men, but being puffed up by the boasts of those who have no experience of goodness, they imagine they will escape the justice of <term>God</term> <note>original: ΘΥ (Θεοῦ); a sacred abbreviation used by scribes</note>, who sees all things and hates evil. 

Often, many of those placed in authority—friends who were trusted to manage affairs—have influenced those in power to become accomplices in the shedding of innocent blood. They have involved them in incurable disasters by deceiving the sincere goodwill of their rulers with the lies of their own malicious character.

---

## Column 3

This can be seen not so much from ancient histories that have been handed down to us, as from what is happening right before your feet. You can see the evils performed by those who are unworthily in power. Therefore, we must look to the future to ensure that the kingdom remains untroubled and peaceful for all people. We will do this by making changes and by judging the matters that come before our eyes with a more reasonable and fair approach.

For Haman, the son of Hamadatha, a Macedonian—who is in truth an alien to Persian blood and far removed from our own kindness—was welcomed by us as a guest. He shared in the humanity we show toward every nation to such an extent that he was proclaimed our "father" and was honored by everyone as the person second only to the royal throne.

---

## Column 4

However, he did not carry this honor with humility. In his pride, he attempted to deprive us of both our authority <note>original: ΠΝΣ (πνεύματος); literally "spirit," here referring to the king's life or sovereign power</note> and our life. By using complex and deceptive methods, he demanded the destruction of Mordecai—our savior and constant benefactor—and Esther, the blameless partner of our kingdom, along with their entire nation. 

Through these schemes, he thought he would leave us isolated and then transfer the sovereignty of the Persians over to the Macedonians. But we find that the Jews, who were handed over for destruction by this thrice-cursed man, are not criminals. Instead, they live by very righteous laws and are the children of the Most High, Greatest, Living <term>God</term> <note>original: ΘΥ (Θεοῦ)</note>. He is the one who has guided the kingdom for us and our ancestors in the most excellent condition. 

Therefore, you will do well not to make use of the letters sent by Haman...

## Column 3

## Column 4

That same day, the number of those killed in Susa was reported to the king. The king said to Esther: "The Jews have killed five hundred men in the city of Susa. How do you think they have fared in the surrounding region? What more do you ask for? It shall be granted to you." 

Esther said to the king: "Let the Jews be permitted to do the same tomorrow, and let them hang the bodies of the ten sons of Haman." The king permitted this to happen, and he gave the order to the Jews of the city to hang the bodies of Haman's sons. 

The Jews in Susa gathered together again on the fourteenth day of Adar and killed three hundred men, but they took no plunder. The rest of the Jews in the kingdom also gathered together to defend themselves and gained relief from their enemies. They killed fifteen thousand <note>The Hebrew Masoretic text records seventy-five thousand</note> of their foes on the thirteenth of Adar, but they took no plunder. They rested on the fourteenth day of the same month and kept it as a day of rest with joy and gladness. 

However, the Jews in the city of Susa gathered on both the thirteenth and the fourteenth days, and did not rest on those days.

## Column 1

...they ceased <note>original: ἀπήλπασαν; they gave up or stopped fighting</note> and rested on the fourteenth day of the same month. They kept that day as a day of rest with joy and gladness. Therefore, the Jews who are scattered in every foreign land keep the fourteenth of Adar as a holiday with gladness, each one sending portions <note>gifts of food</note> to his neighbor. But those who live in the mother cities <note>large metropolitan areas like Susa</note> also keep the fifteenth of Adar as a day of great gladness, sending portions to their neighbors. 

Mordecai wrote these words down in a book and sent them to all the Jews who were in the kingdom of Artaxerxes, both those near and those far away, establishing these days to be observed.

---

## Column 2

<note>Top margin correction: From mourning to joy and from sorrow to a good day.</note>

They were to observe both the fourteenth and the fifteenth days of Adar, because on these days the Jews rested from their enemies. And the month in which their state was turned from mourning to joy and from sorrow to a good day, they were to keep as days of weddings and gladness, sending portions to friends and to the poor. 

The Jews accepted this practice just as Mordecai had written to them: how Haman son of Hammedatha, the Macedonian <note>original: Μακεδὼν; in the Greek text, Haman is often called a Macedonian to emphasize his role as an enemy of the Persian-Jewish peace</note>, had fought against them, and how he had cast a decree and a lot <note>original: κλῆρον</note> to destroy them. They remembered how he went to the king to have Mordecai hanged. However, all the evils he attempted to bring upon the Jews came back upon himself, and he and his children were hanged. 

For this reason, these days were called "Purim" <note>original: Φρουραὶ; likely a Greek transliteration of the Hebrew 'Purim,' meaning lots</note> because of the lots. Because of the words of this letter and all they had suffered and all that had happened to them, they established it.

---

## Column 3

The Jews established and accepted this for themselves, for their descendants, and for all who joined them; they would not use any other way. These days were to be a memorial performed throughout every generation, city, family, and country. These days of Purim <note>original: Φρουραὶ</note> shall be observed for all time, and their memorial shall not fail from among their generations. 

Then Queen Esther, daughter of Aminadab, and Mordecai the Jew wrote down all they had done to confirm the letter of Purim. Mordecai and Queen Esther established this for themselves individually. Then, having established it for their own health and their own counsel, Esther confirmed it by a decree forever, and it was written down as a memorial. 

King Artaxerxes imposed taxes upon the kingdom, both on the land and on the sea. And as for...

Then Mordecai said: "These things have come from <term>God (Θεοῦ)</term>. For I remember the dream I saw concerning these matters; not one word of it has failed to come true. The small spring that became a river, where there was light and sun and much water—this river is Esther, whom the king married and made queen. The two dragons are I and Haman. The nations are those who gathered to destroy the name of the Jews. And my nation, these are the ones who cried out to <term>God (Θεόν)</term> and were saved."

## Column 1

The days for Mattathias to die drew near, and he said to his sons: "Now arrogance and reproach have grown strong; it is a time of destruction and the wrath of anger. Now, my children, be zealous for the law and give your lives for the covenant of our fathers. Remember the deeds of our ancestors, which they performed in their generations, and you will receive great glory and an everlasting name.

However, he saw that the money in the treasuries was running out and that the taxes from the land were small because of the rebellion and the disaster he had brought upon the land by abolishing the laws that had existed from the earliest days. They deliberated about what they should do with the altar of burnt offerings, which had been profaned. A good plan occurred to them: to tear it down, so that it might never be a reproach to them because the nations had defiled it. 

So they tore down the altar and stored the stones on the temple mount in a suitable place until a prophet should come to tell them what to do with them.

So the wedding was turned into mourning, and the sound of their musicians into a lament.

## Column 3

They took full vengeance for the blood of their brother and then returned to the marshes of the Jordan. When Bacchides heard this, he came on the Sabbath day to the banks of the Jordan with a large force. Jonathan said to those with him, "Let us rise up now and fight for our lives, for today is not like yesterday or the day before. Look, the battle is in front of us, and the water of the Jordan is on both sides of us, along with marshes and thickets; there is no place to turn. Now therefore, cry out to <term>Heaven</term> so that you may be saved from the hands of your enemies." The battle began, and Jonathan reached out his hand to strike Bacchides, but Bacchides stepped back from him. Then Jonathan and those with him jumped into the Jordan and swam across to the other side; the enemy did not cross the Jordan after them. About a thousand of Bacchides' men fell that day.

<meta>This page begins the book of 4 Maccabees, transitioning from the historical narrative of 1 Maccabees to a philosophical discourse on the sovereignty of reason over the passions, illustrated by the martyrdoms of Eleazar and the seven brothers.</meta>

## Column 1

As I am about to demonstrate a most philosophical discourse on whether devout reason is master over the passions, I would advise you to attend rightly to philosophy. For this discourse is necessary for everyone seeking knowledge, and it also holds the praise of the greatest virtue, I mean prudence. 

If, then, reason appears to control the passions that hinder self-control, such as gluttony and lust, it also clearly appears to master the passions that block justice, such as malice, and those that block courage, namely anger, fear, and pain. 

"How then," some might say, "if reason controls the passions, does it not master forgetfulness and ignorance?" This is a ridiculous thing to claim; for reason does not control its own defects, but rather those things contrary to justice, courage, and self-control; and these not so as to 

<column-break/>

## Column 2

uproot them, but so as not to yield to them. 

From many places and in different ways I could show you that reason is the sovereign ruler over the passions; but I could prove this much more clearly from the noble character of those who died for the sake of virtue—Eleazar, the seven brothers, and their mother. For all these, looking down upon deaths through torment, demonstrated that reason controls the passions. 

I could speak in praise of the virtues, and of those men who, with their mother, were praised at that time for facing death. I would call blessed those who were so honored. The excellence of these men, who died under torture for their noble courage, was not only admired by all people, but even the tyrants were amazed at their endurance, being themselves the cause of their victory. But also concerning 

-> ENDURANCE <-

<column-break/>

## Column 3

now is the time to speak, if first, as is our custom, we state the thesis for a theoretical discourse on the subject, and then we will turn to their narrative, giving glory to the all-wise <term>GOD (Theō)</term>. 

We seek then to discover if devout reason is the sovereign ruler over the passions, and we define what exactly reason is, and what a passion is, and how many forms of virtue there are, and whether reason masters all of these. 

Reason, then, is the mind with right logic choosing the life of wisdom. Now wisdom is the knowledge of divine and human things and of their causes. This, then, is the training of the Law, through which we learn divine things with reverence and human things with profit. 

The forms of wisdom are prudence, justice, courage, and self-control. Prudence is the most sovereign of these, through which reason masters the passions. The natural forms of passions are pleasures and pains; and each of these 

<column-break/>

## Column 4

<margin>MB</margin> 
naturally concerns both the body and the soul. Many sequences of passions follow both pleasure and pain. Before pleasure is desire, and after pleasure is joy. Before pain is fear, and after pain is distress. 

Anger is a passion common to both pleasure and pain, if one considers how it happens upon distress. In pleasure there is also malicious desire, which is the most versatile of all the passions. 

In the soul, it is arrogance, love of money, love of glory, contentiousness, and envy; in the body, it is eating everything, eating alone, and gluttony. Just as there are two roots and plants of the soul, namely pleasure and pain; and from these plants sprout the vices of the passions, which reason, being like a gardener <note>possible correction on 'being'</note>, by weeding out, cleaning, pruning, binding up, watering, and in every way changing...

## Column 1

...and over all the pleasures that fall into one’s hands. Our reason is the holy master of desires. Now, having first learned that self-control is a restrainer of pleasures, it is clear that it rules over them. The law creates our self-control, which is the mastery of desires. Some desires are of the soul, while others are of the body, and reason appears to rule over both of these. For how else is it that when we are moved toward forbidden foods, we turn away? Is it not because reason is able to master the appetites? For I believe that regarding the life of birds, fish, fowl, four-footed beasts, reptiles, and all forbidden foods according to the law, we overcome them through the mastery of reason.

<column-break/>

## Column 2

For the pleasure of the appetites is restrained by the temperate mind, and all the movements of the body are curbed by reason; and those of the conscience <unclear/> not only that, but they are denied the sharing of beauty. Perhaps Joseph is praised because by reason he masterfully controlled his mind for the sake of chastity. Though he was young and at the peak of his strength for sexual union, he nullified the impulse of the passions by his reason. And it appears that reason masters not only the drive for sexual desire toward women, but every desire. For the law says: "You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife, nor anything that belongs to your neighbor." Indeed, when the law tells us not to covet, it should much more convince us that reason can master desires, just as it can master the passions that hinder justice. For in what way...

<column-break/>

## Column 3

...could one who is by nature a glutton, a gourmand, or even a drunkard be transformed, unless it were clear that <term>the Lord</term> of the passions is reason? For instance, one who lives according to the law, even if he is a lover of money, forces his own character by lending to those in need without interest, and he cancels the debt at the arrival of the seventh year <note>Marginal correction: as it is said</note> by cutting the debt. Even if a man is stingy, he is ruled by the law through reason, neither gleaning the stalks of the full harvest nor the fallen grapes of the vineyards. And regarding the wheat... reason remains the master of the passions. Similarly, it masters the affection toward parents, <note>Marginal mark indicating a textual unit</note> not betraying virtue for their sake. It also masters the friendship toward a wife, turning away from her if she acts lawlessly. It rules over the affection for children, punishing them for their vice, and it dominates the intimacy with friends, rebuking them for their wickedness. And do not think it...

<column-break/>

## Column 4

...extraordinary that reason is able to master even enmity because of the law. Neither should we flee from the domestic animals of enemies... These things are characteristic of enemies: to take cities and to destroy the ranks of horses. Reason appears to master the passions through its strength; and the temperate mind repels all these malicious passions—arrogance, boasting, vainglory, and malice—just as it also controls anger. For reason is yoked with anger... <note>Marginal mark: possibly a quire mark or reference</note> For Moses, when he was moved against those who rose up, though he felt anger, he was seen to be superior to the passions through his understanding. <note>Marginal correction mark</note> It is best to see reason in their transformations. For instance, Jacob the father censured Simeon and Levi regarding their anger, blaming them because they slaughtered without reason, saying, "In their anger..." <note>Final marginal mark</note>

## Column 1

...if reason is not able to master anger. For it did not say that reason masters ignorance, but it fashioned man and planted within him his passions and his dispositions. At that time, He enthroned the sacred guiding mind over all things through the senses, and He gave the law to the mind. By living according to this law, it shall rule a <note>variant for "rule"</note> rule that is temperate, just, good, and brave. How then, someone might ask, does reason prevail if it is over the passions? Does it appear to rule through forgetfulness? Not at all. For by what reason could one say that the mind rules over pure pleasure or pain? Or is it purified of unpleasantness? It is only through reason that we are able to cut off the passions of the soul, for reason is able to help the temper. Some of you might say an evil cannot be cut off, but by not being bent by malice, reason is able to be an ally of logic. Reason roots out some of the passions, but rather it is a contender against them.

<column-break/>

## Column 2

This can be clearly understood through the account of King Antiochus. For when the king sat with his counselors upon a high place and prepared the instruments of torture, he was prepared according to the instruction. From his heart, he would show our own intentions. The rinds and vessels were burned in abundance; I was extended by the soldiers of the nation. Then, when evening came, he hastened like an Ionian to a guard, and they were moved toward the kingdom and the dwelling of the one commanded over the armies for the transaction. On the following day, the king became especially excessive, having every opportunity for the direction of their power. He healed their tyrant. Concerning the desire of the father, this was especially out of desire, and not even a direction. From there it burned, so that none of these things happened even after the king’s desire. For the faith that worships <term>God</term> has conquered. He overcame the king’s entire desire through harsh tortures and wild beasts. And of the oppositions...

For with desire, he now hastens toward the mind by the Savior <note>nomina sacra: SROS</note>; for it has conquered all the passions. Antiochus, called Epiphanes, took the throne <margin>Section 2</margin>. Jason, the brother of Onias, supplanted him in the high priesthood, promising the king through a petition three hundred and sixty talents of silver, and eighty talents from another revenue. When the king agreed and Jason took power, he immediately shifted his fellow countrymen to the Greek way of life. He set aside the royal favors granted to the Jews through John the father of Eupolemus (who had conducted the embassy for friendship and alliance with the Romans), and, abolishing the lawful government, he introduced unlawful customs. For he gladly established a gymnasium right under the citadel itself and brought the noblest of the youths under the Greek hat <margin>Section 4</margin>. There was such an extreme of Hellenism and an advancement of foreign ways, because of the exceeding unholiness of Jason, who was an impious man and no high priest, that the priests were no longer eager for the service of the altar. Instead, despising the Temple and neglecting the sacrifices, they hastened to participate in the unlawful distributions in the wrestling arena after the summons to the discus. They held the honors of their fathers as nothing, but considered Greek glories to be the finest. Because of this, a difficult situation surrounded them, and those whose ways they emulated and whom they wished to be like in everything became their enemies and punishers <margin>Section 5</margin>. For it is no small thing to act impiously against the divine laws, as the coming time will show. # 4 MACCABEES

## Column 1

One of those seized first was a man of noble birth named Eleazar, a priest by birth and a lawyer by profession. He was advanced in age and well-known to many in the tyrant's circle because of his seniority. He was brought out and placed near him. When Antiochus saw him, he said:

"Before I begin to apply the first tortures against you, I would advise you to taste the swine’s flesh and save yourself. I respect your age and your gray hair; yet, after so many years, you seem to me to be no philosopher for following the religion of your people. Why do you loathe this most excellent food, which nature has so graciously provided for the sustenance of our kind? It is quite senseless, I think, and unjust to reject nature’s gifts. It seems even more foolish to me if, because of a misguided idea of the truth, you despise me to the point of your own punishment. Will you not wake up..."

## Column 2

"...from your foolish philosophy and scatter the nonsense of your reasonings? Take up a mind worthy of your years and philosophize according to the truth of what is profitable. Bow before my benevolent festival and have mercy on your own old age. For even if there is an overseeing power in this religion of yours, it will surely grant you forgiveness for any transgression of the law committed under such necessity."

When the tyrant had urged him in this manner to eat the unlawful meat, Eleazar asked for the opportunity to speak. Having received permission to talk, he began his discourse:

"We, O Antiochus, are persuaded that we live by a divine law. We believe no necessity is more powerful than our obedience to that law. Therefore, we do not consider it right to transgress it in any way. Even if, as you suppose, our law were not truly divine..."

## Column 3

"...still we could not rightfully set aside our reputation for piety. Do not think it a small sin to eat forbidden food. To break the law in small things is just as significant as in large things, for in both cases, the law is equally disregarded. You mock our philosophy as if we do not live by sound reasoning. But it teaches us temperance, so that we master all pleasures and desires; it trains us in courage, so that we willingly endure all pain; it teaches us justice, so that we treat all fairly in our customs; and it teaches us piety, so that we worship the only living <term>God</term> with magnificence.

Therefore, we do not eat forbidden things. For we are convinced that the Lawgiver, being the Creator of the world, understands our nature and has permitted us to eat what is compatible with our souls, while forbidding us to eat what is contrary..."

## Column 4

"...to them. But it is tyrannical of you not only to force us to eat defiled food, but also <note>to eat</note> and to break the law so that you can mock us for this hateful violation. You shall not have this laugh at my expense, nor will I break the sacred oaths of my ancestors concerning the keeping of the law. You may cut out my tongue, put out my eyes, and burn my entrails; I am not so old or cowardly that my reason will not remain young for the sake of my piety. Therefore, prepare the torture! I will not abandon the law of my fathers. I will not prove false to you, O Law, nor will I forsake the honorable priesthood and the knowledge of the law. You shall not defile the sacred dignity of my old age. I will not come to you as a living example of one who abandons the law. Even if you kill me, you will not touch my soul..."

## Column 1

Concerning the birth pains she felt for them, this woman, who had given birth to a perfect piety, did not turn away. Neither did she turn when the first son [suffered], nor when the second went before the torturers, nor the third son. Even having seen the sight of each one’s eyes—for she observed the pleasure [they took in their faith] amidst the torments—seeing the same torture and the [mutilation] of their faces, she did not weep. Though she saw the flesh of her children being torn away, and the flesh of her children being hacked off, and hands being cut off at the hands [of the executioners], and heads being severed from their heads, and bodies falling upon dead bodies, and seeing a great [slaughter] of her children’s bodies through the tortures, you did not weep, O pious mother. Not even the nightingale’s song is so filled with maternal love, nor are the sounds that draw in their listeners so [poignant] as the voices of children calling out to their mother from amidst their torments.

Though she was the mother of seven children, she dissolved all her maternal affection through her faith in <term>God</term>. ## Column 1

...sooner than any of the holy ones, she was pained by the lamentation of others. Yet, she was called a lover of life because she invoked <term>God</term>, preserving the memory of those who died. ## Column 4

## Column 1

...not wipe out your every way; and the young men from the streets. And the corpses of <term>men</term> shall be for an example upon the face of the field of your land, like the one who reaps behind the harvester, and there shall be no one to gather them.

Thus says <term>the Lord</term>: let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, and let not the strong man boast in his strength, and let not the rich man boast in his wealth; but let him who boasts boast in this: understanding and knowing that I am <term>the Lord</term>, <note>doing</note> mercy and judgment and righteousness upon the earth, for in these things is my will, says <term>the Lord</term>. 

And I will visit judgment upon all the circumcised who have uncircumcision: upon Egypt, and upon Edom, and upon Moab, and upon the sons of Ammon, and upon all those who cut the hair around their faces, who dwell in the desert; for all the nations are uncircumcised in the flesh, and all the house...

## Column 2

...of Israel are uncircumcised in their hearts.

Hear the word of <term>the Lord</term>, which he has spoken over you, O house of Israel. Thus says <term>the Lord</term>: do not learn the ways of the nations, and do not be afraid of the signs of <term>heaven</term>, for they fear them in their own persons. For the customs of the nations are vain; it is wood cut from the forest, the work of a carpenter and a casting. They are decorated with silver and gold; they have fastened them with hammers and nails, and they will not be moved. 

They go about with beaten silver; it is poured silver from Tarshish, gold from Mophaz, and the hand of goldsmiths; they have clothed them all in gold and silver. Blue and purple is their clothing; they are all the works of craftsmen. 

But <term>the Lord God</term> is true; he is the living <term>God</term> and the eternal King. From his wrath the earth shall be shaken...

<column-break/>

## Column 3

...and the nations shall not endure his wrath.

Thus you shall say to them: the gods who did not make the <term>heaven</term> and the earth, let them perish from the earth and from under this <term>heaven</term>. 

<term>The Lord</term> is he who made the earth by his strength, who set the world right by his wisdom, and by his understanding he stretched out the <term>heaven</term>. And he brought a multitude of water in <term>heaven</term> and brought up clouds from the end of the earth; he made lightnings for rain and brought out light from his treasuries. 

Every <term>man</term> has become foolish from his knowledge; every goldsmith is put to shame by his carved images, because they have cast falsehoods, and there is no <term>spirit</term> in them. They are vain, the works of those who are mocked; in the time of their visitation they shall perish. The portion of Jacob is not like this, for he who formed all things is his inheritance; <term>the Lord</term> is his name. He has gathered from outside...

<column-break/>

## Column 4

...your substance, you who dwell among the chosen ones.

For thus says <term>the Lord</term>: behold, I will trip up those who inhabit this land in affliction, so that your wound may be found. Woe for your crushing; your wound is painful. And I said: truly this is your wound, and it has overtaken me. My tent has become distressed, and all my curtains were torn apart; my sons and my sheep are no more. There is no longer a place for my tent, nor a place for my curtains. 

For the shepherds have become foolish and did not seek <term>the Lord</term>; because of this, the entire pasture did not understand and was scattered. Behold, the sound of a report comes, and a great shaking from the land of the north, to make the cities of Judah a desolation and a nest of ostriches. 

I know, <term>O Lord</term>, that a <term>man's</term> way is not his own, nor shall a man walk and direct his own course. Correct us, <term>O Lord</term>, but...

<summary>Jeremiah contrasts the living God, the Creator of heaven and earth, with the worthless idols manufactured by craftsmen, while lamenting the impending desolation of Judah. The passage ends with a prayer acknowledging that man cannot direct his own path and asking for the Lord's correction.</summary>

-> A Psalm for Asaph <-
<margin>72</margin> How good <term>God</term> is to Israel, to those who are upright in heart.
But as for me, my feet were almost shaken;
my steps had nearly slipped.
For I was envious of the lawless when I saw the peace
of sinners.
For there is no refusal in their death,
and no strength in their affliction.
They are not in the labors of men,
and they shall not be punished along with other men.
Therefore pride has taken hold of them;
they have clothed themselves in their injustice and ungodliness.
Their injustice shall come forth as if from fat;
they have followed the impulses of their hearts.
They thought and spoke in wickedness;
they spoke injustice from on high.
They set their mouth against heaven,
and their tongue went through the earth.
Therefore my people shall return here,
and full days shall be found
among them.
And they said, "How does <term>God</term> know?

<margin>101</margin> <term>Lord</term>, hear my prayer,
and let my cry come to you.
Do not turn your face
away from me;
in whatever day I am afflicted, incline
your ear to me.
In whatever day I call upon you,
quickly hear me.
Because my days have failed like smoke,
and my bones like dry wood
have been burned up.
I was struck like grass and my heart
was withered,
because I forgot to eat
my bread.
From the voice of my groaning,
my bone was joined
to my flesh.
I became like a pelican of the desert;
I became like an owl
in a ruin.
I stayed awake and became like
a lonely sparrow
on a roof.
All day long my enemies reproached
me,
and those who praised me swore
against me.
Because I ate ashes like bread
and mixed my drink with weeping,
from the face of your anger
and your wrath;
because having lifted me up, you dashed me down.
My days declined like a shadow,
and I withered like grass.
But you, <term>Lord</term>, remain forever,
and your memorial to
generation and generation.
You, having arisen, will have mercy on Zion,
because it is time to have mercy on her,
because the time has come.
Because your servants took pleasure in
her stones,
and they will have mercy on her dust.

This passage contains the famous "Acrostic of the Virtuous Woman," though here presented in the Greek Septuagint tradition of the Codex Sinaiticus, which contains notable textual variations from the standard Hebrew Masoretic text.</meta>

## Column 1

Judge righteously and plead the cause
of the poor and the weak.
Who shall find a virtuous woman?
For she is more precious than
costly stones.
The heart of her husband trusts
in her;
such a woman will not
lack fine spoils.
For she works good for her husband
all her life.
Spinning wool and flax,
she made it useful with
her hands.
She became like a ship
trading from afar;
she gathers her livelihood, and
rises during the night,
and gave food to the household and
tasks to the maidservants.
After considering a field, she bought it;
and from the fruit of her hands,
she planted a possession.
Girding her loins strongly,
she applied her arms
to work.
And she tasted that working
is good,
and her lamp is not extinguished
all through the night.
She extends her forearms
to useful things,
and she applies her hands
to the spindle.
She opened her hands to the poor,
and extended her fruit to the needy.
Her husband does not worry
about those in the house when he is away;
for all those with her <note>laby- added by a later hand</note> are clothed.
<note>correction: double</note> She made cloaks
for her husband,
and garments for herself
of fine linen and purple.
Her husband becomes notable
at the gates,
whenever he sits in council
with the elders <note>and elders added below in small script</note>

of the inhabitants of the land.
She made fine linens and sold them,
and belts for the Canaanites.
She opened her mouth
attentively and lawfully,
and she set an order for her tongue.
She clothed herself with strength and dignity,
and rejoiced in the final days.
The ways of her household are orderly,
and she did not eat the bread of idleness.

Her mercy raised up

for a wise woman is blessed,
and let her praise the fear of the <term>Lord</term>.
Give to her from the fruit of
her lips,

<meta>This page transitions from the ending of the Book of Proverbs to the beginning of Ecclesiastes (1:1 through 2:6). The text follows the Septuagint tradition, where the "Preacher" (Ecclesiastes) reflects on the repetitive nature of the world and the vanity of human effort.</meta>

## Column 1

<margin>A</margin> The words of the Preacher, the son of David, king of <term>Israel</term> in <term>Jerusalem</term>.
"Vanity of vanities," said the Preacher; "vanity of vanities, all is vanity."
What profit is there for <term>man</term> in all his labor in which he toils under the sun?
A generation passes away and a generation comes, but the earth stands forever.
The sun rises and the sun sets, and it hurries to its place.
Rising there, it moves toward the south and circles toward the north.
The <term>spirit</term> [wind] goes circling around, and the <term>spirit</term> returns upon its circuits.
All the torrents flow into the sea, yet the sea is not filled; to the place where the torrents flow, there they return to flow again.
All words are wearisome; a man will not be able to speak of it, and the eye will not be satisfied with seeing, nor will the ear be filled with hearing.
What is it that has happened? The very thing that will happen. And what is it that has been done? The very thing that will be done.
And there is nothing new under the sun. Who is he who will speak and say, "Look, this is new"? It has already happened in the ages that were before us.
There is no remembrance of the first things, and even for the last things that happen, there will be no remembrance of them among those who will come at the very end.
I, the Preacher, became king over <term>Israel</term> in <term>Jerusalem</term>, and I gave my heart to seek out and to examine in wisdom all things that happen under heaven; for <term>God</term> has given a miserable distraction to the sons

<column-break/>

## Column 2

of men to be distracted by it.
I have seen all the works <margin>THE WORKS</margin> done under the sun, and behold, all is vanity and a pursuit of <term>spirit</term>.
What is crooked cannot be straightened, and what is lacking cannot be numbered.
I spoke in my heart, saying, "Behold, I have become great and have increased wisdom beyond all who were before me in <term>Jerusalem</term>," and my heart saw much wisdom and knowledge.
And I gave my heart to know wisdom and knowledge; I knew parables and understanding, that this also is a pursuit of <term>spirit</term>.
For in the abundance of wisdom is an abundance of knowledge, and he who increases knowledge will increase pain.
I said in my heart, "Come now, I will test you with mirth, and look upon what is good"; and behold, this also was vanity.
To laughter I said, "It is madness," and to mirth, "Why do you do this?"
I considered whether my heart would draw my flesh like wine, <note>a later hand added "me" above the line</note> while my heart guided me in wisdom, and how to take hold of mirth until I might see what is good for the sons of men, which they should do under the sun during the number of the days of their life.
I magnified my work; I built houses for myself, I planted vineyards for myself, I made gardens and parks for myself and planted in them every kind of fruit tree. I made pools of water for myself to irrigate from them a forest

<summary>This page contains the opening of Ecclesiastes, where the author reflects on the cyclical and "vain" nature of life under the sun. He describes his personal pursuit of wisdom, knowledge, and physical pleasures, ultimately finding them to be a "pursuit of spirit."</summary>

<summary>The Preacher reflects on the divinely appointed times for every human activity and concludes that while human labor is a "distraction" given by God, one should find joy in it as a gift. He observes that God's work is eternal and immutable, and that God will eventually judge both the righteous and the wicked, testing humanity to show their similarity to beasts.</summary>

## Column 1

Let your words be few <note>the scribe originally wrote ΛΟΓΥΩ</note>. For a dream comes through a multitude of trials, and the voice of fools through a multitude of words. 
When you make a vow to <term>God</term>, do not delay to pay it; for there is no pleasure in fools. 
Pay whatever you have vowed. It is better that you should not vow than that you should vow and not pay. 
Do not let your mouth cause your flesh to sin, and do not say before <term>God</term> that it was a mistake, lest <term>God</term> be angry at your voice and destroy the works of your hands. 
For in a multitude of dreams and vanities and many words, you must fear <term>God</term>. 
If you see the oppression of the poor and the violent perversion of justice and righteousness in a province, do not marvel at the matter; for a high official watches over another high official, and there are higher ones over them. 
Moreover, the profit of the earth is for all; the king himself is served by the field. 
He who loves silver will not be satisfied with silver, and who has ever loved a crop in its abundance? This also is vanity. 
When goods increase, those who eat them increase; and what advantage is there to the owner, except to see them with his eyes? 
Sweet is the sleep of a laborer, whether he eats little or much; but the abundance of the rich will not allow him <note>a small 'ι' was added above the 'ι' of 'αφιων'</note> to sleep. 
There is a sickness I have seen under the sun: wealth kept by its owner to his own hurt; and that wealth is lost in a bad

venture. And he begets a son, and there is nothing in his hand. All his days also he eats in darkness, and in much sorrow and anger and sickness and resentment.

## Column 1

He shall live many years, and the number of the days of his years shall be many, yet his soul shall not be satisfied with good, and also he has no burial; I say that a stillborn child is better than he. For it comes in vanity and departs in darkness, and its name shall be covered in darkness. Moreover, it has not seen the sun nor known rest; there is more rest for this one than for the other. Even if he lived a thousand years twice over and saw no good, do not all go to one place?
<margin>></margin> All the labor of <term>man</term> is for his mouth, and yet his soul shall not be satisfied. For what advantage has the wise man over the fool? Or what has the poor man who knows how to walk before the living?
<margin>></margin> Better is the sight of the eyes than the wandering of the soul; this also is vanity and a striving of the <term>spirit</term>.
<margin>></margin> Whatever has happened was already named, and it is known what <term>man</term> is; and he cannot contend with him who is mightier than he. For there are many words that increase vanity.
What advantage is there to <term>man</term>? For who knows what is good for <term>man</term> in his life, during the number of the days of his vain life, which he spends like a shadow? For who can tell <term>man</term> what shall be after him under the sun?
A good name is better than precious oil, and the day of death than the day of one's birth.
It is better to go to the house of mourning than to go to the house of feasting, because this is the end of every <term>man</term>, and the living will lay it to his heart.

---

## Column 2

Sorrow is better than laughter, for by the sadness of the face the heart is made better.
The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, but the heart of fools is in the house of mirth.
It is better to hear the rebuke of the wise than for a man to hear the song of fools.
For as the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of fools; this also is vanity.
And this too is vanity, for extortion makes a wise man mad and destroys the heart of his courage.
The end of a matter is better than its beginning; the patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit.
Do not be quick in your spirit to be angry, for anger rests in the bosom of fools.
Do not say, "Why were the former days better than these?" For it is not from wisdom that you have asked about this.
Wisdom is as good as an inheritance, and an advantage to those who see the sun.
For wisdom is a defense as money is a defense, but the excellence of knowledge is that wisdom gives life to him who possesses it.
Consider the works of <term>God</term>; for who can make straight what <term>He</term> has made crooked? In the day of prosperity be joyful, and in the day of adversity consider: <term>God</term> has made the one as well as the other, so that <term>man</term> should find nothing after him. I have seen all things in the days of my vanity: there is a righteous man who perishes in his righteousness, and there is a wicked man who prolongs his life in his wickedness.
Do not be overly righteous, and do not make yourself overly wise, lest—

<meta>This page continues the text of Ecclesiastes, moving from chapter 7, verse 16 through chapter 8, verse 13. The author reflects on the limits of human wisdom, the nature of righteousness, the necessity of obeying authority, and the mystery of divine justice in the face of wickedness.</meta>

## Column 1

Do not be overly wise, lest you be confounded. Neither be excessively wicked, and do not be stubborn, so that you do not die before your time. It is good that you take hold of this, and from that also do not defile your hand; for he who fears <term>God</term> shall escape all these things. Wisdom helps the wise more than ten rulers who are in the city. For there is no righteous <term>man</term> on earth who does good and does not sin. Also, do not give your heart to all the words that the wicked speak, lest you hear your servant cursing you; for your own heart often knows <note>marginal mark</note> that you also have cursed others. All this I have tested by wisdom. I said, "I will be wise," but it was far from me. That which is far off and exceeding deep—who can find it? I applied my heart to know, to search, and to seek wisdom and the reason of things, and to know the foolishness of the wicked, and the stubbornness and madness of folly. And I find more bitter than death the woman who is a snare, whose heart is a net and whose hands are chains. He who is good before the face of <term>God</term> shall escape from her, but the sinner shall be caught by her. "Look, this is what I have found," says the Preacher, "comparing one thing to another to find the reason, which my soul still seeks but I have not found. One <term>man</term> among a thousand I have found, but a woman among all these I have not found. But look, this only have I found: that <term>God</term> made <term>man</term> upright, but they have sought out many schemes."

---

## Column 2

Who knows the wise? A <term>man's</term> wisdom makes his face shine, and the hardness of his face shall be hated. Keep the king's command, and because of the oath of <term>God</term>, do not be hasty to leave his presence. Do not take your stand in an evil matter, for he will do whatever he pleases, just as a king has authority; and who shall say to him, "What are you doing?" He who keeps a command will experience no evil thing. A wise heart knows the time and judgment, for to every matter there is a time and judgment. For a <term>man's</term> knowledge is great upon him, because he does not know what will be. For as it shall be, who can tell him? No <term>man</term> has authority over the spirit to restrain the <term>spirit</term>, nor is there authority in the day of death. There is no discharge in war, and wickedness will not save the one who practices it. And all this I have seen, and I applied my heart to every work that has been done under the sun, during the time that <term>man</term> has authority over <term>man</term> to his own hurt. And then I saw the wicked brought to their graves, who had come and gone from the holy place; and they were praised in the city because they had acted in this way. <margin>vanity</margin> This also is vanity. Because a sentence against evil-doers is not carried out quickly, for this reason the hearts of the sons of <term>men</term> are fully set in them to do evil. Although a sinner does evil and his life is prolonged from that time, yet I know that it will be well for those who fear <term>God</term>, <margin>so that they fear before his face</margin>

<summary>The author warns against extremes of behavior and reflects on the rarity of true wisdom, while acknowledging that despite the apparent success of the wicked, it is better to fear God. He also emphasizes the absolute authority of kings and the inescapable reality of death.</summary>

## Column 1

...it will be well with those who fear <term>God</term>,
so that they might fear before his face.
But it shall not be well with the wicked,
neither shall he lengthen his days, which are like a shadow,
because he does not fear before the face of <term>God</term>.
There is a vanity which occurs upon the earth:
that there are righteous people who are treated
according to the deeds of the wicked,
and there are wicked people who are treated
according to the deeds of the righteous.
I said that this also is vanity.
And I commended mirth, because there is
nothing better for a <term>man</term> under the sun
than to eat, drink, and be joyful;
for this shall accompany him in his toil
during the days of his life which <term>God</term>
has given him under the sun.
I applied my heart to know wisdom
and to see the business that is done
upon the earth—for even by day and by night
one's eyes see no sleep.
And I saw all the works of <term>God</term>,
that a <term>man</term> cannot find out
the work that is done under the sun.
However much a <term>man</term> may labor to seek it out,
he will not find it; and even if a wise man
claims to know it, he will not be able to find it.
For I took all this to my heart, and my heart
saw all this: that the righteous and the wise
and their deeds are in the hand of <term>God</term>.
Whether it be love or hate, no <term>man</term>
knows all that is before them.
Vanity is in everything.
One fate comes to the righteous

## Column 2

and to the wicked;
to the good and to the bad;
to the clean and to the unclean;
to him who sacrifices and to him
who does not sacrifice.
As is the good man, so is the sinner;
as is the one who takes an oath,
so is the one who fears an oath.
This is an evil in everything done
under the sun: that there is one fate
for everyone. Furthermore, the hearts
of the sons of <term>men</term> are full of evil,
and madness is in their hearts while
they live, and afterward they go to the dead.
For who is there that has fellowship
with all the living?
There is hope, for a living dog is
better than a dead lion.
For the living know that they will die,
but the dead know nothing at all;
they no longer have a reward,
for the memory of them is forgotten.
Their love, their hate, and their envy
have already perished, and they no longer
have a share forever in anything
that is done under the sun.
Go then, eat your bread with joy,
and drink your wine with a cheerful heart;
for <term>God</term> has already approved your works.
Let your garments always be white,
and let your head never lack oil.
Enjoy life with the wife whom
you have loved all the days of your vain life,
which have been given to you under the sun—
all the days of your vanity.
For that is your portion in life and in
your toil which you endure under the sun.
Whatever your hand finds to do,
do it with all your might.

## Column 1

...do it; for there is no work or calculation or knowledge or wisdom in Hades, where you are going.
I returned and saw under the sun: that the race is not to the swift, and the battle is not to the strong; neither is bread to the wise, nor wealth to the intelligent, nor favor to those who have knowledge; for time and chance will happen to them all. For even <term>man</term> does not know his time: as fish that are caught in an evil net and as birds that are caught in a trap, so are the sons of <term>men</term> trapped <note>the sons of men shall be trapped</note> in an evil time, when it falls suddenly upon them.
I have also seen this wisdom under the sun, and it seemed great to me: there was a small city with few men in it, and a great king came against it, surrounded it, and built great siege-works against it. And he found in it a poor wise man, and he saved the city by his wisdom; yet no <term>man</term> remembered that poor man. Then I said: wisdom is better than strength, yet the wisdom of the poor man is despised and his words are not heard.
The words of the wise heard in quietness are better than the shouting of those who rule among fools. Wisdom is better than weapons of war, but one sinner destroys much good.
Dead flies make the perfumer's ointment stink. A little wisdom is more precious than the glory of great folly. A wise man's heart is at his right hand, but a fool's heart is at his left.

## Column 2

And even when a fool walks along the way, his heart fails him, and everything he thinks is folly.
If the spirit of a ruler rises against you, do not leave your post; for healing will stop great offenses.
There is an evil I have seen under the sun, like an error proceeding from the ruler: the fool is placed in great high positions, while the wealthy sit in low places. I have seen slaves on horses and princes walking like slaves <note>upon the earth</note>.
He who digs a pit will fall into it; and a serpent will bite him who breaks through a wall. He who moves stones will be hurt by them; he who splits wood will be endangered by it.
If the iron axe-head falls off, and he has troubled its face, then he must use more strength; and wisdom is an advantage for success.
If a serpent bites before it is charmed, then there is no advantage to the charmer.
The words of a wise man's mouth are grace, but the lips of a fool will swallow him up. The beginning of the words of his mouth is folly, and the end of his talk is wicked madness; and a fool multiplies words.
<term>Man</term> does not know what has happened or what will be; <note>after</note> for who can tell him what will come <note>after</note> him?
The labor of fools wears them out, for they do not even know how to go to the city.

## Column 1

...of a free man, and your princes eat at the proper time, for strength and not for shame.
Through laziness the rafters will sink, and through idleness of hands the house will leak.
They make bread for laughter, and wine and oil gladden the living; but money answers for all things.
Do not curse the king, even in your thoughts, and do not curse the rich in your bedchambers; for a bird of the heavens will carry your voice, and that which has wings will report your word.
Cast your bread upon the surface of the waters, for after many days you will find it.
Give a portion to seven, and even to eight; for you do not know what evil will happen upon the earth.
If the clouds are filled with rain, they pour it out upon the earth; and if a tree falls to the south or to the north, in the place where the tree falls, there it will lie.
He who watches the wind will not sow, and he who looks at the clouds will not reap.
Just as there is no one who knows the way of the spirit, or how the bones grow in the womb of a pregnant woman, so you will not know the works of <term>God</term>, who does all things.
In the morning sow your seed, and toward evening do not let your hand rest; for you do not know which will prosper, whether this or that, or if both alike will be good.
The light is sweet, and it is good for the eyes to see the sun.
For if a man lives many years, let him rejoice in them all, and let him remember the days of darkness, for they will be many. Everything that comes is vanity.

## Column 2

Rejoice, young man, in your youth, and let your heart cheer you in the days of your youth; walk in the ways of your heart and in the sight of your eyes, but know that for all these things <term>God</term> will bring you into judgment. Remove anger from your heart and put away evil from your flesh, for youth and folly are vanity.
And remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the days of trouble come and the years draw near when you will say, "I have no pleasure in them."
Before the sun and the light and the moon and the stars are darkened, and the clouds return after the rain; in the day when the keepers of the house tremble, and the men of power are bent, and the grinders cease because they are few, and those who look through the windows grow dim.
The doors will be shut in the marketplace when the sound of grinding is low, and one will rise up at the voice of a bird, and all the daughters of song will be brought low.
Also, they will be afraid of heights, and terrors will be in the way; the almond tree will blossom, the grasshopper will be a burden, and the caper berry will fail; because man has gone to his eternal home, and the mourners go about the marketplace.
Before the silver cord is snapped, and the golden bowl is crushed, and the pitcher is broken at the spring, and the wheel is broken at the well; and the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to <term>God</term>, who gave it.
Vanity of vanities, said the Preacher; all is vanity.
And moreover, because the Preacher was wise, he still taught the people knowledge; he pondered and sought out a collection of proverbs.
The Preacher sought to find pleasant words and what was written uprightly—words of truth.
The words of the wise are like goads, and like firmly fixed nails are the collected sayings given by one Shepherd.
And beyond these, my son, be warned: of making many books there is no end, and much study is a weariness of the flesh.
Let us hear the conclusion of the whole matter: fear <term>God</term> and keep His commandments, for this is the whole duty of <term>man</term>. For <term>God</term> will bring every deed into judgment, including every hidden thing, whether it is good or whether it is evil.

## Column 1

The immortality of virtue is known before <term>God</term> and before men;
when it is present, they imitate it,
and they long for it when it has departed.
And throughout eternity, it marches wearing a crown, <margin><note>mark and marginal word QUICKLY</note></margin>
having won the contest for the prizes of purity.
But the many-offspringed multitude of the ungodly will be of no use,
and from illegitimate seedlings,
it will not strike a deep root
nor establish a firm foundation.
For even if it blossoms in its branches for a season,
standing insecurely, it will be shaken by the wind,
and by the force of winds, it will be uprooted.
Their unfinished branches will be broken off,
and their fruit will be useless,
unripe for eating
and fit for nothing.
For children born of unlawful sleeps
are witnesses of wickedness against their parents
when they are examined.
But if the righteous man should die early, he will be at rest;
for honorable old age is not measured by length of time,
nor is it measured by the number of years.
But understanding is gray hair for humanity,
and a blameless life is the maturity of old age.
Having become well-pleasing to <term>God</term>, he was loved <margin><note>textual mark</note></margin>
and while living among sinners, he was taken away.
Lest wickedness should change his understanding
or deceit should mislead his soul;
for the fascination of evil obscures what is good,
and the wandering of desire undermines an innocent mind.
Being made perfect in a short time, he fulfilled long years;
for his soul was pleasing to the <term>Lord</term>,
therefore He hurried him out from the midst of wickedness.
But the people saw and did not understand...

When I enter into my house, I will find rest with her; for her company has no bitterness, and living with her brings no pain, but rather gladness and joy. ## Column 1

When they were being disciplined, though in mercy, they understood how the ungodly were being tormented while judged in wrath. For you tested your own people as a father admonishing them, but the others you examined as a stern king condemning them. Whether they were absent or present, they were distressed alike; for a double grief seized them, and a groaning at the memory of past events. 

For when they heard that through their own punishments the others were being benefited, they perceived the <term>Lord</term>. For the one who had long ago been cast out and rejected with mockery, they marveled at in the end of these events, having suffered a thirst unlike that of the righteous.

In exchange for their senseless and wicked thoughts, by which they were led astray into worshiping irrational reptiles and worthless vermin, you sent a multitude of irrational animals upon them for vengeance, so that they might know that by whatever means someone sins, by those same things they are also punished.

For your almighty hand, which created the world out of formless matter, did not lack the means to send a multitude of bears against them, or fierce lions, or newly-created beasts full of rage, unknown before—either breathing out a fiery breath, or puffing out a roar of smoke, or flashing terrible sparks from their eyes. Not only could the harm from these creatures have destroyed them, but even the sight of them could have killed them with fear. 

Even without these, they could have fallen by a single breath, pursued by justice and scattered by the breath of your power; but you have ordered all things by measure, number, and weight.

# Wisdom of Solomon

## Column 1

...but the penalty that always follows the transgression of the unrighteous.
But you, our <term>God (Theos)</term>, are kind and true, patient, and governing all things in mercy.
For even if we sin, we are yours, for we know your power.
But we will not sin, knowing that we are accounted as yours.
For to know you is complete righteousness, and to know your power is the root of immortality.
For neither did the evil, wicked invention of men deceive us, nor the fruitless labor of painters—a form stained with varied colors, 
the sight of which leads a fool to desire, and he longs for the form of a dead, soulless image.
Lovers of evil things are worthy of such hopes—both those who make them, those who desire them, and those who worship them.
For a potter, kneading soft earth with much labor, shapes each vessel for our service.
But from the same clay he shapes both the vessels that serve clean purposes and their opposites, all in the same way.
As to what the use of each of these shall be, the worker in clay is the judge.
And with evil labor he shapes a vain god from the same clay—he who was made of earth a short time ago and after a little while goes to the place from which he was taken, when the debt of his soul is demanded.
But he is not concerned that he is destined to die, nor that his life is short; instead, he competes with goldsmiths and silversmiths, and mimics those who work in bronze, and thinks it a glory that he shapes counterfeit things.

---

## Column 2

His heart is ashes, and his hope is cheaper than dirt, and his life is of less value than clay.
Because he failed to know the one who shaped him and inspired him with an active soul and breathed into him a living <term>Spirit (Pneuma)</term>.
Instead, they considered our life to be a game, and our existence a profitable festival; for they say, "One must get gain from anywhere, even from evil."
For this man knows better than anyone else that he is sinning when he creates fragile vessels and carved images from earthly matter.
But all the enemies of your people, who oppressed them, are most foolish and more miserable than the soul of a child.
For they even considered all the idols of the nations to be gods, which have neither the use of eyes for seeing, nor nostrils for drawing breath, nor ears to hear, nor fingers on hands for touching; and their feet are useless for walking.
For a <term>man (anthrōpos)</term> made them, and one who has borrowed his own <term>Spirit (Pneuma)</term> shaped them.
For no man is able to shape a god like himself.
Being mortal himself, he works a dead thing with lawless hands.
For he is better than the objects of his worship; for he indeed lived, but they never did.
Furthermore, they even worship the most hateful of animals; for when compared in their foolishness, these are worse than the others.
Nor are they even beautiful enough to be desired by sight, but they have escaped both the praise of <term>God (Theou)</term> and his blessing.

He conquered the crowd, not by physical strength or the force of weapons, but by his word he subdued the punisher, reminding him of the oaths and covenants of the fathers. For when the dead had already fallen in heaps upon one another, he stood in between and held back the wrath, and cut off the way to the living. For on his long robe was the whole world represented, and the glories of the fathers were on the engraving of the four rows of stones, and Your majesty was upon the diadem on his head. To these things the destroyer yielded, and these things they feared; for the mere trial of Your wrath was enough.

But for the ungodly, a pitiless anger came upon them until the end. For He knew even their future actions beforehand: that after they themselves had permitted them to depart and had sent them on their way with haste, they would change their minds and pursue them. For while they still had their mourning in their hands and were lamenting at the graves of the dead, they adopted another line of reasoning, and those whom they had cast out with entreaties, they pursued as fugitives. For the necessity they deserved drew them to this end, and made them forget what had happened, so that they might fill up the punishment that was lacking in their torments. Since many and great things have been given to us through the Law and the Prophets and the others who followed after them, for which it is necessary to praise <term>Israel</term> for instruction and wisdom; and since not only must those who read become knowledgeable themselves, but also those who love learning must be able to be useful to those outside, both by speaking and writing; my grandfather <term>Jesus</term>, having given himself even more to the reading of the Law and the Prophets and the other ancestral books, and having acquired sufficient mastery in them, was himself also led to write something of the things pertaining to instruction and wisdom, so that those who love learning, having also become familiar with these things, might progress much more through living according to the Law. ## Column 1

<note>+</note> Lend to your neighbor in his time of need,
and in turn, pay your neighbor back on time.
Keep your word and be faithful to him,
and at all times you will find what you need.
Many treat a loan as a stroke of luck,
and they cause trouble for those who helped them.
Until a man receives a loan, he will kiss the lender’s hands,
and he will speak with a humble voice about his neighbor’s money;
but when it is time to pay it back, he will stall for time,
he will offer nothing but listless excuses,
and he will blame the circumstances.
Even if he is able to pay, the lender will hardly get back half,
and he will count even that as a stroke of luck.
But if the borrower does not pay, he has defrauded the lender of his money,
and the lender has gained an enemy for no reason.
The borrower will pay him back with curses and insults,
and instead of honor, he will give him dishonor <note>addition of "and"</note>.
Many, therefore, have refused to lend—not out of wickedness,
but because they were cautious <note>Correction: "u" added above the first vowel to form "they were cautious"</note> and afraid of being defrauded for nothing.
<note>+</note> Nevertheless, be patient with a humble man,
and do not keep him waiting for your charity.
Help the poor for the sake of the commandment,
and because of his need, do not send him away empty-handed.
Lose your silver for the sake of a brother and a friend,
and do not let it rust under a stone until it is lost.
Store up your treasure according to the commandments of the Most High,
and it will profit you more than gold.

<column-break/>

## Column 2

And this treasure will deliver you from every affliction;
it is better than a mighty shield or a heavy spear;
<note>+</note> it will fight for you against the enemy.
A good man will go surety for his neighbor,

Do not forget the kindness of your guarantor,
for he has given his very life for you.
A sinner will ruin the good deeds of a guarantor,
and an ungrateful person will, in his mind, abandon the one who saved him.
Suretyship has destroyed many who were once prosperous,
and has shaken them like a wave of the sea.
It has driven powerful men from their homes,
and they have wandered among foreign nations.
A sinner who falls into suretyship
and chases after business contracts will fall into lawsuits.
Help your neighbor according to your power,
but take care that you yourself do not fall.
<margin>Section 2</margin> The basic necessities of a <term>man's (anthropos)</term> life are water, bread, and clothing,
and a house to cover his nakedness.
Better is the life of a poor man under a roof of beams
than magnificent food in the houses of others.
Be content with little or much,
and you will not hear the reproach of being a stranger.
<note>+</note> It is a miserable life to go from house to house,
for wherever you stay as a guest, you will not dare to open your mouth.
You will entertain and give drink to ungrateful people,

"Come here, stranger, set the table,

"Go away, stranger, to make room for a guest of honor;

These things are hard for a <term>man (anthropos)</term> of understanding to bear:
the reproach of a household and the insults of a moneylender.

## Column 1

->CONCERNING CHILDREN<-

He who loves his <term>son (Υἱὸν)</term> will discipline him with the whip constantly, so that he may rejoice in his later years. <note>+</note> He who disciplines his <term>son (Υἱὸν)</term> will <margin>be praised</margin> benefit from him, and he will boast about him among his acquaintances. He who teaches his <term>son (Υἱὸν)</term> will make his enemy jealous, and he will rejoice over him in the presence of friends. When his <term>father (Πατήρ)</term> dies, it is as if he has not died, for he has left behind one like himself. <note>+</note> In his life, he saw him and was glad, and at his death, he was not grieved. He left behind an avenger against his enemies and one who returns favors to his friends. He who pampers a son will have to bind up his wounds, and his heart will be troubled at every cry. An unbroken horse turns out stubborn, <margin>DISORDERLY</margin> and a son left to himself turns out reckless. <note>+</note> Pamper a child and he will terrify you; play with him and he will grieve you. Do not laugh with him, lest you suffer with him and grind your teeth in the end. Give him no authority in his youth, but beat his sides while he is a child, lest he become stubborn and disobey you. Discipline your son and work with him, so that you do not stumble because of his shameful behavior. A poor man who is healthy and strong in constitution is better than a rich man who is afflicted in his body. Health and fitness are better than any gold, <note>+</note> and a robust body is better than boundless wealth.

## Column 2

->CONCERNING FOOD<-

<note>+</note> There is no wealth better than the health of the body, and there is no gladness above the joy of the heart. <note>+</note> Death is better than a bitter life <margin>or a persistent illness</margin> or a persistent illness. Good things poured out before a closed mouth are like offerings of food placed upon a grave. What benefit does an offering give to an idol? For it can neither eat nor smell. So is the one who is afflicted by the <term>Lord (Κυρίου)</term>, seeing with his eyes and groaning, just like a eunuch embracing a virgin and groaning. Do not give your soul over to sorrow, and do not distress yourself with your own counsel. <note>+</note> Gladness of heart is the life of a <term>human being (ἀνθρώπου)</term>, and the joy of a man is length of days. Love your soul and comfort your heart, and keep sorrow far from you. For sorrow has destroyed many, and there is no benefit in it. Jealousy and anger shorten one's days, and worry brings on old age before its time. <note>+</note> A cheerful and good heart is concerned with food, and takes care of its meals. The sleeplessness of wealth wastes away the flesh, and the worry of it drives away sleep. The worry of sleeplessness prevents slumber, and a very severe illness wakes one from sleep. The rich man toils in the gathering of money, and in his rest, he fills himself with his luxuries. The poor man toils in a meager life, and in his rest, he remains in need.

## Column 1

"You have spoken like one of the foolish women. If we have accepted good things from the hand of the <term>Lord</term>, shall we not endure the bad things?" In all these things that happened to him, Job did not sin with his lips before <term>God</term>.

Now when his three friends heard of all the evils that had come upon him, they each arrived from their own country to visit him: Eliphaz the king of the Temanites, Bildad the tyrant of the Shuhites, and Zophar the king of the Naamathites. They came to him with one accord to comfort and visit him. When they saw him from a distance, they did not recognize him; and crying out with a loud voice, they wept, each one tearing his robe and sprinkling dust upon their heads. They sat with him for seven days and seven nights, and none of them spoke, for they saw that his affliction was terrible and very great.

After this, Job opened his mouth and cursed his day. Responding to the day on which he was born, he said: "Let the day perish <margin>DAY</margin> on which I was born, and the night in which they said, 'Behold, a male!' Let that night be darkness, and let the <term>Lord</term> above not seek it, nor let light come upon it. Let darkness and the shadow of death seize it; let a gloom come upon it. Let that day be cursed, and let it not be counted among the days of the year, nor let it be reckoned in the changing days of the months. Let that night be sorrowful, and let no gladness or joy come upon it. But let the one who curses that day curse it—he who is about to overcome the great sea monster. Let the stars of that night be darkened."

## Column 2

"...let it remain closed <note>unclear text</note> and not see the morning star rising. Because it did not shut the gates of my mother's womb; for that would have removed pain from my eyes. For why did I not die in the womb? Why did I come out from the belly and not perish immediately? Why did knees meet me? And why did I suck at the breasts?

For now I would have been lying down and quiet; having fallen asleep, I would have been at rest with kings and counselors of the earth who took pride in their swords; or with princes who had much gold, who filled their houses with silver. Or I would be like a miscarriage coming out of a mother's womb, or like infants who never saw the light. There the wicked have quenched the fire of their anger; there those exhausted in body have found rest. Together those of old did not hear the voice of the tax collector. Small and great are there, and the servant who no longer fears his <term>Lord</term>.

For why is light given to those in bitterness, and life to souls in pain? They long for death and do not find it, digging for it as if for treasures; they would be overjoyed if they should find it. Death is a rest for a man, for <term>God</term> has hedged him in. For groaning comes to me before my food. I weep, being gripped by fear; for the fear I worried about has come upon me, and what I dreaded has met me. I have neither peace, nor quiet, nor rest; but wrath has come upon me."
