## Column 1

...but wrath has come upon me. 
Then Eliphaz the Temanite replied and said: 
"Has a word often been spoken to you in weariness? But who can withstand the force of your words? 
For if you have instructed many, and encouraged the hands of the weak, 
and raised up the ailing with your words, 
and provided strength to the faint-hearted with weak knees— 
but now trouble has come upon you and touched you, and you are troubled. 
Is not your fear based on folly, 
and your hope, and the wickedness of your way? 
Remember then, who ever perished being innocent? 
Or when were the upright utterly destroyed? 
<margin>ϗ</margin> Just as I have seen those who plow mischief, 
and those who sow it, reap sorrows for themselves. 
By the command of <term>God</term> they shall perish, 
and by the <term>Spirit</term> of his anger they shall be consumed. 
The strength of a lion and the voice of a lioness; 
the boasting of dragons is extinguished. 
The ant-lion perished for lack of food, 
and the lion’s cubs left one another. 
If any true word had been in your speech, 
none of these evils would have happened to you. 
Shall my ear not receive extraordinary things from him? 
With fear and a noise at night, 
when fear falls upon <term>men</term>, 
shuddering and trembling met me, 
and shook my bones greatly. 
And a <term>Spirit</term> came over my face; 
my hair and flesh bristled. 
I stood up and did not recognize it;</column-break/>

## Column 2

I looked, and there was no form before my eyes, 
but I heard a breeze and a voice: 
'What then? Can a mortal be pure before the <term>Lord</term>? 
Or can a man be blameless by his works?' 
If he does not trust his own servants, 
and has noticed something crooked in his angels— 
how much more those who inhabit houses of clay, 
of which we ourselves are made, from the same clay; 
he has struck them like a moth. 
And from morning until evening they are no more; 
they perished because they could not help themselves. 
For he breathed on them and they withered; 
they perished for lack of wisdom. 
Call out then, if anyone will answer you, 
or if you will see any of the holy angels. 
For wrath kills the foolish man, 
and envy slays the one who has gone astray. 
I have seen the foolish taking root, 
but suddenly their dwelling was consumed. 
Let his sons be far from safety; 
let them be crushed at the gates of lesser men, 
and there shall be no one to deliver them. 
For what they gathered, the righteous shall eat; 
but they themselves shall not be delivered from evils; 
let their strength be drained away. 
For trouble does not come out of the earth, 
nor shall pain sprout from the mountains; 
but <term>man</term> is born to toil, 
just as the young of vultures fly to the heights. 
Nevertheless, I will make my petition to the <term>Lord</term>, 
and I will call upon the <term>Lord</term>, the Master of all, 
who does great and unsearchable things."

## Column 1

...glorious and extraordinary things, of which there is no number. 
He gives rain upon the earth and sends water upon all that is under <term>heaven</term>. 
He raises the lowly to a high place and lifts up those who are lost. 
He thwarts the counsels of the crafty, so that their hands do not achieve success. 
He catches the wise in their own wisdom and overwhelms the counsel of the devious. 
By day they meet with darkness, and at noon they grope as if it were night. 
May they perish in war, and may the weak escape from the hand of the powerful. 
So there may be hope for the weak, and the mouth of the unjust shall be shut. 
Blessed is the <term>man</term> whom the <term>Lord</term> has reproved; do not reject the discipline of the Almighty. 
For he causes pain and restores it again; he strikes, and his hands heal. 
Six times he will deliver you from distresses, and in the seventh no evil shall touch you. 
In famine he will rescue you from death, and in war from the power of the sword. 
He will hide you from the scourge of the tongue, and you shall not fear coming evils. 
You shall laugh at the unjust and the lawless, and you shall not fear wild beasts. 
For wild beasts shall be at peace with you. 
Then you will know that your house shall be at peace, and the life of your tent shall not fail. 
You will know that your seed is many, and your children shall be like the grass of the field. 
You will go to the grave like ripe grain harvested in its season, or like a heap of a threshing floor gathered in its time.

## Column 2

<note>Let us see if he is still near</note>
Behold, we have searched these things out; these are the things we have heard. 
But you, know for yourself what you have done. 
Then Job answered and said: 
"If only someone would truly weigh my anger and lift my pains in a balance together! 
Indeed, they would be heavier than the sand of the seashore; but as it seems, my words are worthless. 
For the arrows of the <term>Lord</term> are in my body, whose wrath drinks up my blood; 
when I begin to speak, they pierce me. 
For why? Will a wild donkey bray for nothing, unless it is seeking food? 
Or will an ox low at the manger when it has fodder? 
Will bread be eaten without salt? Or is there any taste in empty words? 
For my soul cannot rest, for I see my food as the stench of a lion. 
Oh, that my request might come to pass, and that the <term>Lord</term> would grant my hope! 
Let the <term>Lord</term> begin and wound me, but let him not destroy me utterly. 
Let the grave be my city, upon whose walls I leaped; 
for I will not give up; 
for I have not lied about the holy words of my <term>God</term>. 
For what is my strength, that I should endure? 
Or what is my time, that my soul should persist? 
Is my strength the strength of stones? 
Or is my flesh made of bronze? 
Or have I not trusted in him? 
But help is far from me. 
Mercy has rejected me, and the oversight of the <term>Lord</term> has disregarded me. 
My closest friends have not looked upon me; 
like a failing brook or like a wave they have passed me by. 
Those who used to respect me now fall upon me. 
Like snow or frozen ice, which was not known before, 
so I too have been abandoned by everyone."

## Column 1

I was rejected and became like a house; but you have not been kind to me. For those who judge do not distinguish between flesh. And you have not been a shame to your friend. You fall upon me and seek my property. But even you have set upon me pitilessly. So, seeing my wound, be afraid. For why? Have I asked anything of you? Or do I lack your strength, so that you should save me from enemies or rescue me from the hand of the powerful? Teach me, and I will be silent; if I have erred, tell me. 

But as it seems, the words of a true man are worthless. For I do not ask for strength from you, nor will your rebuke convince me with words. For I will not endure the sound of your speech. Except that you fall upon the orphan and leap upon your friend. But now, looking into your faces, I will not lie. Sit down now, and let there be no injustice; and again, let there be no injustice in the righteous. For there is no injustice on my tongue; or does my throat not meditate on understanding? 

Is not the life of <term>man</term> on earth a trial? And his life is like that of a daily hireling, or like a servant fearing his <term>Lord</term> <note>originally written as KY but corrected to KN</note> and having found shade, or like a hireling waiting for his wages. So I also have endured empty months, and nights of pain have been given to me. If I lie down, I say, "When will it be day?" And when I rise again, "When will it be evening?" I am full of pains from evening until morning. My body is covered in the rot of worms.

<column-break/>

## Column 2

I waste away into clods of earth from my discharge. My life is lighter than a word and has perished in a new hope. Remember that my life is <term>breath</term>, and my eye shall no longer return to see good. The eye of him who sees me will not look around at me. Your eyes are upon me, and I am no more. Like a cloud cleared from heaven, if a <term>man</term> goes down to Hades, he shall never come up again. He shall not return to his own house <note>repetition of "own" in the original</note>, nor shall his place know him anymore. 

Therefore, I will not spare my mouth; I will speak while being in distress; I will open the bitterness of my soul <margin>3</margin>, being held by fear. Am I the sea or a dragon, that you have set a guard over me? I said that my bed will comfort me, and I will privately bring a word to myself upon my couch. You terrify me in my sleep and strike me with visions. You will release my soul from my <term>breath</term>, and my bones from death. For I shall not live forever, that I should be patient. 

Depart, leave me alone, for my life is vain. For what is <term>man</term>, that you have magnified him? Or that you set your mind upon him? Or that you make a visitation of him until morning? How long will you not let me be, nor let me go until I swallow my spittle in pain? If I have sinned, what can I do to you, O you who know the mind of <term>men</term>? Why have you set me as your target? And I am a burden to you. And why have you not caused my lawlessness to be forgotten, and a cleansing of my sin? For now I shall depart into the earth.

"Truly I know that it is so; for how can a mortal be righteous before the <term>Lord</term>?

For the wicked die a strange death, but the righteous are mocked.

## Column 2

Life [is short] and full of wrath.
Like a flower that has bloomed, it falls away;

For there is hope for a tree;
if it is cut down, it will bloom again,
and its sprout will not fail.
For even if its root grows old in the earth,
and its stump dies in the rock,
at the scent of water it will bloom;
it will produce a harvest like a new plant.
But a man who has died is gone;
and when a mortal falls, he is no more.
For in time the sea is diminished,
and a river becoming deserted is dried up.
But <term>man</term> having fallen asleep shall not rise,
until <term>heaven</term> is no longer sewn together,
and they shall not be awakened from their sleep.

and set a time for me in which you would remember me!
For if a <term>man</term> dies, shall he live?

You have numbered my practices,

You have sealed up my sins in a pouch;
and you have noted if I have transgressed unintentionally.

and a rock will grow old [and wear away] from its place.

For there is a place from which silver comes, and a place for gold from where it is filtered. Iron is made from the earth, and copper is quarried like stone. # ΙΩΒ (Job)

He is mighty in the strength of his heart; he will not preserve the life of the ungodly, but he will grant justice to the poor. <meta>This page provides the editorial notes and the index for the 1911/1922 facsimile edition of Codex Sinaiticus, mapping the manuscript's folios and columns to biblical references in Swete's "The Old Testament in Greek."</meta>

->NOTES TO INDEX<-

GENERAL NOTE. In the compilation of the index, the chapter and verse in Swete's edition of "The Old Testament in Greek" have been followed throughout.

Note a. Where the manuscript is fragmentary, the verse with which a fragment ends has been given in addition to the first verse. Where a column continues after a gap in the manuscript, the gap is represented as x, followed by the number of the verse where the column immediately resumes.

Note b. On page 7* column 4, at line 26 (KC), 2 Esdras 9:3 begins immediately after the ending of 1 Chronicles 19:17.

Note c. Swete conveniently designates the unnumbered portions of "Esther" as (A, B, etc.).

Note d. In Swete's numbering of the N text of Tobit, 14:15 precedes 14:8. This numbering has been followed in the index.

Note e. Page 118* column 2 begins with the introductory verse (omitted by Swete) immediately preceding Lamentations 1:1.

Note f. The headings (not numbered by Swete) that prefix the various sections in N are numbered in the index as part of the following verse.

Note g. In the numbering of Ecclesiasticus 30–36, Swete's numbering has not been followed in the index. The unbracketed numbers represent those of the manuscripts of the Septuagint; the bracketed numbers represent those of the Old Latin versions, etc., and indicate the actual position of the text in Swete's edition.

->All small letters in the columns below refer to the notes above.<-
